Gārbā (Gujarat)
Ghamar (Rajasthan)
Hoḷi (Manipur)
Kolāṭa (Karnataka)
Lūḍi (Punjab)
Paṅgi (Himachal Pradesh)
Suggi-kuṇita (Karnataka)
Tabal Coṅgbi (Manipur)
Tiyān-bāghi (Punjab)

There is no gainsaying the fact that dances have not only enriched our national culture but have also added a new dimension of joy and pleasure to the life of our masses.
Drama
According to the Nāṭyaśāstra of भरत, मुसिच् and dancing are an integral—but subsidiary—part of nāṭaka or drama. However, both of them gradually developed into independent streams of art. Drama, on the other hand, continued to retain them also as its parts.
Drama, as an item of social एदुचतिओन् and entertainment, must have originated at a very early period. The Ṛgvedic mantras wherein a ṛṣi, under the exciting influence of सोम juice, challenges इन्द्र to fight with him, or, another one pathetically describes his fate brought about by his weakness for गम्ब्लिन्ग्, point to the histrionic talents inherent in many human beings.
The basic theme of a drama is expressed through conversations and मुसिच् with appropriate acting. The total effect will be enhanced by proper dress, ornaments and equipment. All these are dealt with in the Nāṭyaśāstra of भरत.
For the enactment of a drama, a suitable place, called ‘raṅgasthala,’ was necessary. It could be triangular, square, circular or semicircular in shape depending on the availability of space. It was generally divided into two parts: the raṅgabhūmi (stage) and the prekṣāgṛha (auditorium). During the earlier period, these two parts used to be of equal dimensions.
The stage had a green-room, a back stage and a front stage as also a rest room at the side. Screens were very much in use.
Dresses and ornament as also different hair-styles appropriate for the roles played have been described in detail in the works of नाट्यशास्त्र. Masks also were in use.
The themes of the dramas in ancient days might have been chosen from the mythological literature. With the advent of classical Sanskrit literature, social themes too might have become popular as evidenced by the dramas of कालिदास, भवभूति (8th cent.), Śūdraka (3rd cent.) and others.
There is reason to believe that the dramatic art might have branched off into two streams—the refined type for kings, courtiers and the elite of the society; the folk-type meant for the masses.
It may safely be assumed that dramatics was a well-developed art in India even during the beginning of the christian era.
11. हिन्दु चुल्तुरे Outside India
Introduction
The desire for conquest is inherent in human beings. Conquest, however, can be of two types: physical conquest through war and violence; cultural conquest through the head and the heart. Histories of nations over the centuries have proved that it is the latter that survives whereas even the traces of the former may be thrown out when the conquered nation rebels and reasserts itself, regaining its lost freedom.
The cultural conquest has another, a tremendous, advantage. The heart can mellow the head when the latter displays arrogance. And, the head can harden the former if it leads to debilitating sentimentalism.
The way हिन्दु चुल्तुरे, based on the multifaceted Hindu religion, has quietly spread far beyond the geographical boundaries of India, proves this theory. It is the sages and savants, sans the Sword and sans the Book, that went out of this country to other regions of the globe to spread the message of universal love and brotherhood. They were least interested in political colonization or accumulating wealth through trade and commerce. India had plenty of military power and wealth. In fact it is the latter that tempted the foreigners from the Middle-East and the West to set off a series of savage invasions against this country. That neither the Hindus nor their religion and culture were wiped out of this land—on the other hand, they are still going strong—is proof enough of the wonderful religio-cultural resilience of the Hindus.
Right from the beginning of the Christian era, if not earlier, Hindu religion and culture have spread to all parts of Asia, and some parts of the Middle-East as also Siberia and the Americas. It will be interesting to study this phenomenon to enrich our own knowledge of the same.
For the sake of easy comprehension the presentation can be made according to the countries, arranged in the alphabetical order.
Afghanisthan
The गान्धार Deśa of the epic period has been identified with the present-day Afghanisthan. The name of the Kandahar city seems to confirm this.
Two images of गणेश have been found in this country:
One at Gardez (belonging to the 6th century A. D.);
Another at Sakar Dhar near Kabul (belonging to the 4th century A. D.). Here, images of सूर्य and शिव (7th century A. D.) also have been discovered.
The colossal image of बुद्ध near Bamiyan, measuring 53 meters (177 ft.) is another standing monument of Indian culture. 18
America
Christopher Columbus (A.

-1506) is said to have discovered America. But, did he, really? May be, but only for Europe! He discovered a few small islands between the two huge American continents and a small part of the Honduran coast!
But, millennia before that, the Americas had not only been discovered but had also been covered with large settlements of Indian (Hindu) population. The Aztecs of Central Mexico, the Incas of Peru and Mayas of Yucatan (South-East Mexico) were all Hindu settlers from

They believed in the four युगस्, had adopted the गुरुकुल system of एदुचतिओन्, the pañcāyat system of village administration and the bazaar economy, performed सोम sacrifices, worshipped इन्द्र, गणेश and other Hindu deities, were well-versed in Hindu religious dances, practised the rituals usually associated with child-birth, मर्रिअगे and death, and had the priestly hierarchy too.
Arabia
Hewitt, in his monumental work Ruling Races of Prehistoric Times 20 (Vol. II), gives an elaborate account of Hindu rule in Arabia and Mesapotamia.
Will Durant, in his well-known book, The Story of Civilization (Vol. IV, The Age of Faith, New York, Simon and Schuster, pp. 161-171) writes that within the Kaaba, in the pre-Moslem days, there were several इदोल्स् and that one was called ‘Allah,’ which was probably the tribal god of the Quraish. During the festival and पिल्ग्रिमगे seasons, ‘kanyās’ or unmarried girls, took part in dancing.

It is now a well-recognized fact that the Arabs were responsible in propagating in Europe, the literature and knowledge they had acquired from India, like the Pañcatantra and several treatises on subjects such as mathematics, अस्त्रोनोम्य्, medicine and surgery and so on.
Bali and Jāva
Hindu religion and culture started spreading to the various islands of South East Asia even from the first century A. D. Some of the kings of South India who were defeated by their rivals, migrated to the islands like जाव and established their own kingdoms there.
Known as Yavadvīpa, probably from the 10th cent. A. D., जाव was the home of well-known dynasties of kings like Śrīvijaya Rāja.
The work Ajiśaka states that during the first century A. D., twenty thousand people from कलिङ्ग (Orissa, India) came and settled down in the island of जाव.
A very large number of Hindu scriptural works in Sanskrit (excepting the वेदस्) written in the Kawi script have been discovered. The following list can give an idea of the same:
Purāṇas (Mythology): Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa, Viṣṇu-purāṇa
Mantraśāstra (Rituals and Worship): Sūryasevana (pūjā of शिव and आदित्य); several mantras connected with ritualistic worship; Mṛtyuñjaya and गायत्री mantras; some hymns like Viṣṇustava.
Nītiśāstra (Ethics): Sārasamuccaya of वररुचि Ādipurāṇa; Kāmandaka Nītiśāstra.
Dharmaśāstra (Social Science): Śivaśāsana; Kuṭāra Mānavāgama; Devāgama; Svarajambu
Vyākaraṇa (Grammar): Ādisvara; Amaramālā; Vṛttasañcaya.

Apart from these there is the famous Rāmāyaṇa Kakawin in old Javanese. Works on medicines, अस्त्रोलोग्य्, stories and literary classics and history works have also been found. The Rāmakavaca (22 verses in Sanskrit) appears to be quite popular even now.
Śaivism made its first appearance in जाव around 4th century A. D. The oldest image of गणेश has been found on the Dieng plateau. Another image found near Borobudur is considered to be the finest.
The residents of the island of बलि are all Hindus even today. They follow the वर्ण-आश्रम system. उपनयन ceremony and सन्ध्या ritual are being observed even now.
Shadow-plays, puppet-shows and Bharatanāṭya with Hindu mythological themes are still in vogue.
Borneo (Indonesia)
Around the 5th century A. D. हिन्दुइस्म् had already penetrated into Borneo. An epigraphical record discovered at Kotei describes the performance of some Hindu rites there. Most of the images discovered in Borneo are either Śaivite (including a गणेश image) or Buddhist. A Sanskrit inscription on a yūpastambha (pillar of sacrifice used in Vedic rituals) has also been found and has been attributed to Mūlavarma (A.

. The Vikramarāja dynasty and the Sukhodaya kingdom came into existence in the 8th and the 9th centuries.
King Poonnareeka (Puṇḍarīka?) who ascended the throne of the Pegu dominion in 746 A. D. was considered as a lover of ब्राह्मणस्. It was he who built the city of Ramanago (City of राम). The Rangoon City of today stands on the same site.
The people of Pegu were known as the Mons and also as Talaiṅgs, thereby suggesting their migration from the Telengana region of Andhra Pradesh.
With their knowledge of अस्त्रोलोग्य् and other sciences, the ब्राह्मणस् among the Talaiṅgs held important positions even in the courts of the Buddhist kings. While performing religious ceremonies on special occasions such as चोरोनतिओन् of a king or laying the foundation for a new building, they had introduced the worship of नारायण.
There are good reasons to believe in the existence of a विष्णु temple at Pagan, from an inscription engraved on sand-stone, containing a Sanskrit verse from the famous Mukundamālā Stotra of कुल-śekhara, but in the ग्रन्थ स्च्रिप्त्.
The Burmese law-books, called Dhammathats, are based on the Manu-smṛti. They are still recognised as valid legal authority regulating इन्हेरितन्चे and other domestic disputes.
Cambodia (Kampuchia)
Known as Kambuja-deśa in our paurāṇic literature, the first kingdom of Cambodia is said to have been established by one Kauṇḍinya, a disciple of Aśvatthāma. He married a नाग princess, Somā by name, built a capital Bhavapura and started the Somavaṁśa line of Hindu rulers there.
The great sage अगस्त्य from South India, is reputed to have spread the Hindu religion and culture in the entire South East Asia and is highly revered in Cambodia even now.
Numerous inscriptions—most of them in faultless Sanskrit—have been found in Cambodia, confirming the spread of Hindu religion and culture.
Both the भागवत (Vaiṣṇava) and the Śaiva cults were popular. Temples of शिव and गणपति exist even now. There was very good understanding between the Buddhists and the Hindus. Even by the 6th century A. D., study of the वेदस्, recitation of Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and some पुराणस्, was quite common. Tantras like Jayadrathayāmala and Niśśvāsa-saṁhitā were in vogue. Princes of the royal families were educated in the Sanskrit grammar of पाणिनि, Siddhāntas (Śaiva?), धर्मशास्त्रस् and the darśanas also, apart from all secular fields of knowledge needed by them.
Among the हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस्, the अन्ग्कोर् वत्, near the city of Angkor Thom 23 (built by the king Sūryavarman II, A.

-1152) is the most famous.
The Bayon Vat, also in Angkor Thom, is a Buddhist temple of colossal dimensions built by Jayavarman VII (A.

-1215). The large towers exhibit gigantic masks of Bodhisattva Lokeśvara on the four sides of each and everyone of the towers.
Campā (South Annam, part of Vietnam)
Known as Campādeśa in the various Sanskrit inscriptions of that country, it is now a part of Vietnam, its South Annam region. The impact of हिन्दु चुल्तुरे must have started as early as the 2nd century A. D. The important centres of the ancient kingdom of Indo-China were: अमरावती (Quangnam), विजय (Bin-dinh); Kauthara (Nhatrang); पाण्डुरङ्ग (Phan-rang).
A bronze image of बुद्ध found at Dong-Duong (known earlier as Indrapura) is in the Amaravati style of sculpture. It is 1.08 metres (43 inches) in height and is assigned to the period A.

.
The oldest king, according to an inscription discovered at Vo-Canh, belonged to the Śrīmāra dynasty (3rd cent. A. D.). A new dynasty was established by Rudravarman (A.

-572) belonging to a ‘brahma-क्षत्त्रिय’ family.
Another monarch, Bhadravarman by name (early 5th cent. A. D.), is said to have built a temple for शिव (‘Bhadreśvara-svāmin’ ) at the site now identified with Mison. The temple site of Mison contains ruins of over seventy small and big buildings constructed from time to time by the kings of चम्पा.
Pṛthvīndra Varman (A.

-820) were the other kings who were famous for their benign rule.
A four-armed standing image of गणेश has also been discovered in the same site, near a शिवलिङ्ग. स्कन्द (Kumāra or सुब्रह्मण्य) was also a popular deity, not only with the masses but also with the rulers.
A number of हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस्, belonging mostly to the 10th century A.D., are found in the same area. Some of them are still in a good condition.
Cīnā (China)
Unlike the influence of Hindu religion and culture on the countries of South East Asia, Indian influence on Cīnā or China has been confined almost entirely to the spread of बुद्धिस्म्. According to one view, images of बुद्ध made in India, were found even during the early period of the Hān dynasty (121 B. C.). बुद्धिस्म् is said to have been introduced into China during the rule of Emperor Ming in A.
. History of the Liyang dynasty mentions the arrival of ambassadors from India during the years A.

to 167.
A galaxy of scholarly Buddhist मोन्क्स् started visiting China right from A.

. To mention a few: कश्यप Mātaṅga, Dharmaratna, Mahābala and धर्म-phala. They settled in the Lo-yang province and spent most of their time in translating many Buddhist works 24 into the Chinese language.
The greatest of such scholars was Kumārajīva (A.
-413). He arrived in Chang-an during A.

and before his death in 413, had translated several Buddhist works including the more famous ones like the Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras and Saddharma-puṇḍarīka.
The other Indian scholars who did notable work of translation are: Paramārtha (A.

-774).
That a large number of Chinese travellers visited India from time to time for higher studies in बुद्धिस्म् is now a well-recognised fact of history. Among them the following were more well-known for their life and work: Fahien (A.

-713).
It is interesting to note that गणेश pictures have been discovered on wooden panels and frescoes in Khotan in West China, suggesting the spread of हिन्दुइस्म् at an early period.
Iran (Eastern part)
Iran—known earlier as Persia—was the home of Zoroaster (6th cent. B. C.) and his religion, Zoroastrianism or the Pārsi religion, which has a great affinity to the early Vedic हिन्दुइस्म्.
According to the account of some Chinese travellers, the Hīnayāna बुद्धिस्म् was prevalent in Persia and that the vessel which बुद्ध was using to beg his ड़ोओद्, had been preserved in the store-होउसे of the king. 25
Al-Beruni (A.

-1039) has stated that in former times Khorasan, Persia, Iraq, Mosul and the country up to the frontier of Syria were Buddhistic.
During the 7th century A. D., there was a regular exchange of envoys between the king Khusru of Persia and Pulakeśin II in South India.
The late king of Iran, the Shah, who was dethroned and forced to leave the country, belonged to a ruling dynasty called ‘Pahlavas’. The Pahlavas are a race of kṣattriyas mentioned in Vedic legends. वाल्मीकि, बालकाण्ड, 54.18.">26 It is also interesting to note that his royal title, ‘Ārya-mihir’ (‘the Sun of the Aryan race’) is a pure Sanskrit word!
The well-known story of the descent of the गङ्गा river from हेअवेन् has found an important place in the Zend Avesta, the scripture of Zoroastrianism, in the pre-Islamic Iran.
The Yazidis—also spelt as Yezdis—are a confederation of tribes and have a religion based on Zoroastrianism. Kurdish, Turkish and Arab tribes are included in this group. They have the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् (4 castes, similar to the 4 varṇas), practise monogamy, believe in the transmigration of souls and revere fire. 27
Japan
Buddhism entered Japan via China and Korea. It gradually replaced Shintoism the native religion of Japan.
The word ‘Zen,’ in ‘Zen-बुद्धिस्म्,’ which became extremely popular in Japan is a corrupt form of the Sanskrit word ‘dhyāna’. Being a combination of Buddhist teachings and Taoist म्य्स्तिचिस्म्, it teaches meditation on the Śūnya or the Great Void, reminiscent of the Nirguṇa ब्रह्मन् of Advaita Vedānta.
The Buddhist temple complex Horyūji, near नर (South Honshu, Japan) is the oldest in Japan. It contains mural paintings of Buddhas and lesser figures, all in the अजन्ता style.
Contacts Japan had with ancient India are also confirmed by the Japanese beliefs and stories such as a hare living on the मोओन्, the story of the crocodile, the monkey and his liver, and, the ऋष्यशृङ्ग legend that was developed as an opera, The Story of Monoceros.
Huge icons of बुद्ध prepared during the period A.

also bespeak of the spread and popularity of बुद्धिस्म्.
Korea
Korea had contact with India right from the 4th century A. D. बुद्धिस्म् was brought to Korea from China by a भिक्षु, Soondo by name, in A.

, during the reign of king Sosoorimwang.
The first Indian teacher—whose Korean name was Ahdo 28—arrived in A.
and two temples were built in A.
at Pyongyang. Ten years later, the second Indian teacher, Mallānanda, came to Korea. The third one—Mookhoja by name—is said to have visited Korea during A.

.
Gradually different sects were established. Both the king and the people started constructing temples and vihāras (Buddhist monasteries) with images and painting of बुद्ध and other divinities.
The manufacture of sacred utensils used in worship and other works of art contributed to the development of various fine-arts.
In course of time, the Korean scholars introduced not only बुद्धिस्म्, but also certain arts, crafts and literature into Japan.
Kymik was probably the first priest of Korea to visit India and bring several Buddhist scriptures of the Vinaya school. Six more visited India later.
Kwanrenk of Paikje was an eminent scholar who went to Japan and established the famous Horyūji temples there.
Wunchenk (A.

-696) of Silla was a great Sanskrit scholar responsible for establishing a special school of बुद्धिस्म्.
Around the 8th century A. D. the ध्यान (Zen) cult was introduced into Korea.
Construction of caves and stūpas like those in India, some musical instruments in use like the flute and mohtahk (ghaṇṭā or bell) as also temple bells bespeak of Indian influence on Korean art and architecture.
The Koryuh dynasty (A.
to 1391) built and restored temples, stūpas and monasteries. The greatest achievement of these kings is the production of the Mahādharmakoṣa (A.
), an encyclopaedia of बुद्धिस्म्, through scholars in their court. When it was destroyed by the invading Mongols, another edition was produced in A.

.
The Hanguel script of Korea was developed, based on the phonetic system of Sanskrit in A.

.
Indian culture has had a great influence on many aspects of Korean culture, whether art or architecture, literature, मुसिच् or dance.
Laos
Originally known as ‘Lava,’ Laos is one of the countries of South East Asia, deeply influenced by India. As per archaeological evidence and Chinese records, the Hindus colonised and established their kingdoms not only in Burma but also in the upper valleys of Chindwin river (in Burma or Myanmar), the Irawadi and the Salween rivers (also in Burma) as also the Mekong and the Red River areas (in South East Asia). There is evidence that a Hindu kingdom existed in Laos also. The earliest known historical king was Śrutavarman and then his son Śreṣṭhavarman. 29 The capital of the kingdom, the Śreṣṭhapura was located around Vat Phu Hill near Bassac (in Laos).
The earliest material evidence of ancient Hindu influence goes back to the 6th century A. D. The Vat Phu Hill near Bassac was then called Liṅgaparvata. A temple of Bhadreśvara शिव is said to have existed there.
In Laos, there are many figures of बुद्ध with certain Indian traits like the hair on the head being treated in small curls or the nāsāgradṛṣṭi (gaze being fixed on the tip of the nose).
The scriptural art as also architecture of Laos also shows Indian influence as seen in the Vat Pa Ruok and Vat Ban Tan temples. They contain Gupta-Cālukyan features. The monastery Ban Peng Thai exhibits certain traits prevalent in medieval Kerala. Window frames of big buildings clearly show Hindu influence. The Vat Pra temple (17th cent A. D.) is adorned by an image of लक्ष्मी standing on a lotus, over its dome!
The पाली language was common till the 16th century.
The Indian गुरुकुल system exists in Laos even now.
Malaya (Malaysia)
India’s ties with Malaysia are closer and older than is generally recognised. By the similarities between the glass beads discovered in the Malay peninsula and those at the Hallur site of Dharawad in Karnataka, the contact between the two peoples must have been from 1000 B. C.
The Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, the Niddesa (a पाली canonical text belonging to a late B. C. era), the Jātakas, the Milindapanha, the Śilappadikāram (in Tamil), the Raghuvaṁśa of कालिदास and a host of other ancient literary works contain reference to India’s association with South East Asia including Malaya.
A Hindu king of Śrīvijaya (a maritime kingdom in Indonesia that lasted from the 7th to the 13th centuries) had already established his supremacy over parts of Malaya even by A.

Mexico The migration of Hindus and Buddhists from India to the Americas (from Alaska to the Andes), their establishing colonies there and spreading their religion and culture millennia before Columbus is now a well-recognized fact. The Americanist Congress held in the Mexico City in 1962, where a number of learned papers supporting this theory were presented, is the proof of this. The material concerning the religions and cultural ‘invasion’ of the Americas, especially of Mexico and Peru, is so abundant that we can give only a very brief outline of the same here: The Aztec चलेन्दर् followed by the ancient inhabitants was based entirely on the four Yuga-system of the Hindus. The people followed the वर्ण-आश्रम system, especially under the Inca rulers. The extent of the empire was 1.5 lakh square kilometers and the population 20 millions. The ceremonial dances of the natives as discovered by the Spaniards in A.

, were closely related to and resembled Hindu dances.
The process of च्रेमतिओन् of the dead, closely resembled that of the Hindus.
Temples of Mexico—as for instance, the one at Tajin—were typically Hindu. The remains or ruins bear testimony to the same.
Archaelogical monuments of Mexico bear unmistakable resemblance to हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् or Buddhist stūpas.
Hindu images of gods like शिव, गणेश, इन्द्र, वामन and नरसिṁह, Vānara (monkey) heroes and आदिशेष, traditional temple motifs like lotus and lions, as also Buddhist images and wheels have been found in many places. Worship of some of these gods too existed.
The गुरुकुल system of एदुचतिओन् was very much in vogue.
Monogamy and arranged marriages were common. Astrologers were consulted before मर्रिअगे. मर्रिअगे ceremonies were simple and similar to the Hindu customs. Seeing the pole-star (by the couple) was a must.
The devadāsī system was prevalent. Girls dedicated to the temple deity were expected to tend the sacred fires in the temples which were never extinguished.
Belief in a life after death and transmigration of souls was a part of their philosophy.
Widows of kings often practised sahagamana or सती.
Coronation ceremonies of kings were elaborate religious rites, very similar to those of the ancient Hindu kings.
Dasara festival was celebrated in commemoration of राम’s victory!
Other signs of हिन्दु चुल्तुरे are: the family system including joint-families, āyurvedic doctors and their herbal remedies, the bazaar system, the cooperative system during social and religious ceremonies, sun- worship and so on.
Nepal
Nepal is the only Hindu kingdom of the world existing today. Culturally it has been connected with the Indo-Gangetic plains for over 2500 years. Lumbiṇī, the birthplace of बुद्ध, is in Nepal.
The Kirātas ruled Nepal from the 3rd century B. C. to the 5th century A. D. The लिच्छविस् ruled from A.

. Then it was the turn of the Mallavi race. All of them were Hindu rulers.
Temples and stūpas of Nepal derived their inspiration from India and Tibet.
The temple of Paśupatinātha on the bank of the Bāgmatī river, to the east of Kathmandu is a famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे even now, for the Hindus of India. There are numerous other shrines in its vicinity.
The Rādhākṛṣṇa temple at Patana is known for its grandeur.
The गणेश temple at Zimpi Tandu, assigned to the period A.

, is also famous.
An image of Virūpākṣa-शिव of the pre-Christian era has also been found.
A beautiful wooden image of a deity with twelve hands at a temple in भक्त-pura exhibits the special features of Nepali sculpture.
Inscriptions are available from the 5th century A. D., right up to the 12th century. The script is similar to the one used in the Gupta period (4th to 6th centuries A. D.). Coins issued by the Licchavi kings are similar in format and ornamentation to the Gupta coins of India.
The Nepali language written even now in the देवनागरी script is a metamorphosed form of Sanskrit. It is much nearer to Hindī, Gujarātī and Sindhī.
Peru
It is Peru in South America—as Mexico was in the North—that has had the maximum impact of Hindu religion and culture even from the most ancient days. The Incas of Peru were none other than the Hindus who had migrated by land and sea from India.
The temple of Sun at Kushko (Cuzco)—since converted into a church—built of immense blocks of stone, is a marvel of engineering and architecture. When the Spanish invaders plundered the temple they found immense wealth there.
The Incas—who were Sūryavaṁśis—believed in the four युगस्. Their अस्त्रोनोम्य् was similar to that of the Hindus. Their almanacs were known as ‘Panchacta Unnanchae (c.f. with the word ‘pañcāṅga’).
The Incas were great builders of temples, roads, rest-houses and other public structures. Their transport system was very good. Their textiles were unequalled during their days.
Hindu paurāṇic beliefs and images of gods like सूर्य, Ādikūrma, Anantanāga, goddess मय (mother of the gods) are found in Peru even now.
There was a sacrament called ‘Hauracu’ which every boy at puberty had to undergo. This was remarkably similar to the उपनयन ceremony of the Hindus.
The Quichua (Keśava?) language of the Peruvians has hundreds of words which are analogous to Sanskrit.
Some of the prayers of the Inca rulers of Peru appear to be, almost, a replica of certain Vedic hymns. They were used during the fire-ceremonies, resembling the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
Philippines
Indian cultural influences must have arrived in the Philippines through Malaya, Indonesian archipelago and Borneo, any time during the period 200 B. C. to A.

.
The native language of the Philippines was deeply influenced by Sanskrit through the highly Sanskritised Malay language inscriptions of a monarch of the Śrīvijaya dynasty around the 7th century A. D.
Archaelogical evidence also supports the influx of Indian influence. The clay medallion of Avalokiteśvara-Padmapāṇi of Southern Luzon, the bronze Lokeśvara image of Cebu, and the golden गरुड pendant of Brooke’s Point—all assigned to the period 12th to the 14th centuries—confirm this view. Śaiva images too have been found.
The Cham alphabets of the Philippines have been shown by scholars of Indology to be of South Indian origin, resembling the Pallava scripts.
The Moros of Southern Philippines were originally Hindus. The hair-style of women resembles that of Kerala in India. Gold ornaments too have an unmistakable stamp of Indian origin.
Soviet Russia
Startling discoveries of Hindu and Buddhist remnants in Soviet Russia have been disclosed in a recent article by S. K. Malhan in the Indian Express dated Sunday the 27th November, 1983. 31
Soviet archaeologists have found the remains of a giant Buddhist cave- monastery inside the Kara-Tepe Hill in Termez (now in Uzbekistan).
According to the traveller Huoi-Tsao (A.

) who visited the areas near Termez, the king and the nobility of the State, Huo To Lo (or Huttal), believed in the बुद्ध. There were many Buddhist monasteries there. An ancient manuscript discovered there, mentions the restoration of the Buddhist temples in Samarkhand (in Uzbekistan) in the middle of the 7th century A. D.
The excavations have revealed not only cave-constructions but also other buildings including shrines, temples, stūpas and cells. The cave-temples contain genre paintings of various deities and scenes from legends.
Of particular interest is the discovery of inscriptions in different languages including the ब्राह्मी and the खरोष्ठी scripts.
Frescoes and images of बुद्ध, several Sanskrit manuscripts, pieces of silk and paper too have been recovered from the place.
A Vedic fire-temple has been found at Baku on the Capsian Sea (Azerbaijan).
In the Tajikistan region of Russia, carvings depicting a Vedic chariot and other things have been found. 32
The Russian and the Lithuanian languages are very close to Sanskrit.
A Sanskrit text of आयुर्वेद as also a bronze idol of a Vedic deity found in Russia have been displayed at the International Academy of Indian Culture in New Delhi.
Some artifacts recovered from the Adighai people, a Vedic community still surviving in Russia, include bronze axes, इदोल्स् of विष्णु and some decorative figures. They are on display in some Russian museums. The folk-songs and dances of the community as also their oranaments smack of strong Hindu influence.
The Russian carnival of the बुरिअल् of Kupalo (= Cupid, Kāmadeva), lighting of a bonfire and performance of Kolo dance is very much reminiscent of the होलि festival of India with its Kāmadahana (burning of the god of lust) ritual.
Śrī लङ्का (Ceylon)
Śrī Laṅkā—Siṁhaḷadvīpa or Ceylon—has always had intimate and lasting contact with India, both culturally and politically. The prehistoric cultural remains of Śrī लङ्का and the ones discovered at the excavation sites of Teri in Tirunelveli of Tamil Nadu are identical.
As per the epic Rāmāyaṇa, it was the kingdom of रावण.
The राम-सीता episode is very popular in the cultural and social life of the country even now.
The arrival of Prince विजय from the Gujarat area of India in 543 B. C. at Śrī लङ्का marks the historical beginning of Hindu religion and culture. He established a kingdom of his own. Worship of the Hindu gods which are very common even now—Śiva, विष्णु, स्कन्द and Gaṇeśa—might have been introduced from his times.
Aśoka’s (247-207 B. C.) missionaries brought बुद्धिस्म् to Śrī लङ्का.
Buddhaghoṣa brought the tooth-relic of बुद्ध during the regime of Mahānāmā (A.

-431). During this period Gupta culture deeply influenced the art and culture of the island.
During the later period—7th to the 16th centuries A. D.—the Pallava, the Coḷa, the Pāṇḍya and the Vijayanagara empires maintained close links with Śrī लङ्का.
Śaivism seems to have been the dominant religion here along with बुद्धिस्म्. The latter had absorbed विष्णु as the protecting deity of its faith! Worship of स्कन्द (Subrahmaṇya or कार्त्तिकेय) also became quite popular.
The Siṁhalese script and language were deeply influenced by the Indian impact. The impact has also been considerable on the art and architecture, the Barhut, the Sāñcī and the अमरावती styles being more pronounced. Dance and drama too have heavily drawn upon the Bharatanāṭya style.
The चस्ते स्य्स्तेम्, मर्रिअगे customs and dress patterns have the South Indian—especially of Tamil Nadu and Kerala—imprint on them.
Sumātra
The island of Sumātra, is a part of the Indonesian archipelago. Hence it shares the ancient and medieval history of other parts such as जाव, बलि and Borneo. In Sungve Batu a temple as also images of शिव, दुर्गा, गणेश and नन्दि have been found. In Takuvapa, icons of विष्णु and some Vaiṣṇava deities have been discovered.
Even by the 4th century A. D. Sumātra was part of the Śrīvijaya empire. The Laigore inscription speaks of its being a centre of बुद्धिस्म् too.
Thailand (Siam)
Thailand, known formerly as Siam, had been having contacts with Hindu India right from the 2nd century A. D. Recent archaeological discoveries at Prah Pathom and Pong Tak include a bronze image of गणपति (of 6th century A. D.), images of बुद्ध (of अमरावती school of sculpture) and other articles of Gupta style of art and architecture. An inscription in Sanskrit belonging to the 4th century A. D., and some images of Vedic gods too have been found in these sites.
Hindu religion and its scriptures, its language and literature were well-spread during this period. Sage अगस्त्य was highly honoured.

, the first king assuming the title ‘Rāmādhipati.’ Its capital was Dvārāvatī. बुद्धिस्म् was the main religion during the period of this dynasty. However, construction of stūpas and sculpturing of बुद्ध’s icons as also हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् in new styles was encouraged by the rulers.
The Thai (or Siamese) language has, even now, many Sanskrit words, though in a distorted form.
Tibet
Tibet was known as Triviṣṭapa in the ancient days. Before the entry of बुद्धिस्म् through Buddharakṣita, Bon, an animist cult, was the dominant religion of Tibet.
Buddhism became the main religion by the 7th century A. D. when Thonmi Sambhoṭa, the court minister of the then ruler, was sent to India for higher studies. After many years, he returned to Tibet, innovated the Tibetan script, translated many works into the Tibetan language and was the inspiration behind the two encyclopaedic works—the Kangyur and the Tengyur.
Guru Padmasambhava, a famous tāntric teacher from India, visited Tibet in the 8th century A. D. and preached the Vajrayāna doctrine.
During this period, the king being Khri-srom-lde-btsan (A.

-786), Buddh-ism became the State religion. Again, it was during this period that great scholars Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla—apart from Padmasambhava—were brought to Tibet.
On the advice of Padmasambhava, the king sent a body of मोन्क्स् from Tibet to India. The Sam-ye monastery also was built during this period.
In course of time, Tibetan बुद्धिस्म् developed into five major sects or Orders. Several monasteries also grew up with huge libraries and several sublime paintings and images. The now famous मन्त्र Om maṇipadme hum has formed the basis of Tibetan Buddhist practices.
Tibetan art, comprising many images of Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, शाक्त and Buddhist deities, mostly out of copper and bronze, resembles those of the नालन्दा period. The paintings on silk cloth and walls are of the अजन्ता style.
Conclusion
The foregoing brief survey of the spread of हिन्दु चुल्तुरे in various parts of the world confirms the observations made in the beginning of this chapter, viz., that it spread not by the power of the Sword and the Book of Crusaders, but by the power of life and wisdom of the great men of this country, fired by the missionary zeal of the spirit of ‘vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam’ (‘the whole world is your family!’). Strangely enough, not even the names of many of these ambassadors of love and peace, are known to us now!
Though much of this influence has been overshadowed or uprooted by the barbaric invasions of the Semitic races, the traces still surviving are enough to reflect the glory of हिन्दु चुल्तुरे.
